extra.message: The HTTP request path (self.path) is concatenated directly onto the server's working directory and opened with no canonicalization. The traversal filter at line 10-11 only blocks paths that literally start with '/../../', so a single '..' segment (e.g. GET /../../../etc/passwd or GET /..%2f..%2fetc/passwd) or any traversal not anchored at the very start of the path bypasses the regex. The resulting path is passed straight to open() and its contents are returned to the client, allowing arbitrary file read outside the web root.

cwe: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

extra.message: The unsanitized 'post_id' value is concatenated directly into a raw SQL string passed to conn.execute(), instead of using the parameterized form used elsewhere in this file ('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = ?', (post_id,)). Although a weak regex (line 67) attempts to restrict post_id to digits, the concatenation itself is the injectable sink and the surrounding code is explicitly labeled '# Bad: Vulnerable to SQL Injection' / '# SQLI vuln, passes user input to string' by the author, confirming intent and exploitability of this code path if reached.

Multiple SQL query construction patterns concatenate/format an untrusted 'username' variable directly into the query string (string concatenation, .format(), % formatting, and f-string), all of which allow SQL injection instead of using parameterized queries (cursor.execute(query, (username,))).

The 'url' request parameter is validated with a naive str.startswith('https://insecurewebapp.com') check before being fetched with urllib.request.urlopen(url). This check is trivially bypassed with URLs like 'https://insecurewebapp.com.attacker.com/', 'https://insecurewebapp.com@attacker.com/', or 'https://insecurewebapp.com/../../@attacker.com', allowing an attacker to make the server issue requests to arbitrary internal or external hosts (SSRF).

context.check_hostname is explicitly set to False before wrapping the socket in TLS, disabling hostname verification on the server certificate. This allows a man-in-the-middle attacker with any valid certificate (for any domain) to impersonate 'website.com' and intercept/modify the connection.

The payment signature is computed as sha256(secret + payment_information) instead of a proper MAC (e.g. HMAC-SHA256). Because plain SHA-256 is vulnerable to length-extension attacks, an attacker who observes a valid (payment_info, signature) pair can compute a valid signature for payment_info + attacker_suffix without knowing 'secret', letting them tamper with payment parameters (e.g. amount) undetected.

cwe: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

extra.message: Same length-extension flaw as length_extension_attack.py: the signature is sha256(secret + payment_information) rather than an HMAC. An attacker can append arbitrary data (e.g. modify the payment amount) to payment_information and compute a matching valid signature without knowing the secret, bypassing the payment integrity check.

cwe: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

extra.message: When a 'username' cookie is present, the handler is designed to base64-decode the cookie value and pass it to pickle.loads() (documented inline: 'Calls pickle.loads on user supplied info ... No signature present ... enable code execution'). Deserializing an attacker-controlled pickle blob from a client-supplied cookie with no integrity check allows arbitrary code execution via crafted __reduce__ payloads.

The session_id cookie is AES-CBC encrypted/decrypted with no accompanying MAC/HMAC to verify integrity. Because the ciphertext is unauthenticated, an attacker can flip bits in the cookie or exploit a CBC padding oracle (the decrypt() failure path returns a distinguishable 500 response) to tamper with or forge the decrypted 'username' value used for authentication display.

cwe: CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature

extra.message: Flask's SECRET_KEY, used to cryptographically sign session cookies and flash messages, is hardcoded to the weak literal 'qwerty12345'. Anyone with source access can forge signed session cookies.
Flask's SECRET_KEY, used to cryptographically sign session cookies and flash messages, is hardcoded to the weak literal '55555'. Anyone with source access can forge signed session cookies.
